text: a million evaluations to price an option on 100 stocks, an average over 100 inputs. Spread them as a grid, that feels thorough. How many values does each input get? One, the whole grid is one point, the center, two values per input would take two to the hundredth points. Since Metropolis and Ulam's 1949 paper, The standard tool has been random points, like this one. How far off would a million random points land? Start with two inputs. Our function is one inside this quarter disk, zero outside. Its average is exactly one half. A grid of 100 points puts 52 inside, two points off. 100 random darts put 44 inside, six points off. In two dimensions, the grid wins. Now give each a million points and add inputs. The disk becomes a ball, grown to cover exactly half the box. The grid's million points give each axis a thousand values in two dimensions, then a hundred, ten, three. From twenty dimensions on, just the center inside the ball. So the grid's estimate is the whole box. Fifty points off. Even two values on 19 axes is 18 points off, while the darts stay under a tenth of a point. Maybe darts win by giving every axis more values. A million points on the diagonal give every axis a million values and still miss by 8 points. Their coordinates move in lockstep A dart coordinates are drawn independently and uniformly so it lands inside with a chance equal to the answer in any dimension Each dart is a coin flip. One flip is either 0 or 1. Its average is a half, so every flip misses by exactly a half. Repeat the 100 dart experiment 300 times. In both, the estimates spread this wide. Those misses fall up or down at random, so they partly cancel. 16 darts stray about 4 halves, not 16. N darts stray about root N halves. Divide by N, and the typical miss is a half over root N. For 100 darts, 5 points. We measured 4.8. Any other function swaps the half for its own spread, sigma. There's still no D. So back to our ball. A million darts, any dimension. How far off is a typical estimate? One half over a thousand, five hundredths of a point. In 2012, Berkstra and Bengio found random search tuned neural networks as well as grid search, in a fraction of the time. If one setting matters most, nine grid trials test three values of it, nine random trials test nine. Darts do have a blind spot, tiny answers, keep the ball's radius at one, and in 30 dimensions it fills two parts in a hundred trillion of the box. Below this line, a million darts expect under one hit, so they usually report zero. The darts never notice the axes. A million coin flips in any dimension.
